Cool-flame researchCrew protection
Know what is being counted. This is a curated catalog, not the total number of NASA fire experiments. Named investigations and mission campaigns are counted once; individual burns, ignitions, and test runs are separate measures. The five SoFIE titles describe a published portfolio; reviewed sources do not establish completion of all five.

Safety issues

A fire on the ISS threatens both the crew and the air they depend on.

🫁

Toxic combustion gases

Burning materials release gases such as carbon monoxide into the shared cabin air.

How the risk is reduced

Breathing protection limits crew exposure. Gas monitors help identify contamination.

🌫

Smoke and particles

Ventilation carries smoke through a module. Particles can reduce visibility and enter the lungs.

How the risk is reduced

Particle filters capture smoke. Airflow design helps route smoke toward detectors.

🔥

Unexpected fire spread

Ventilation can feed a flame with oxygen and change the direction it travels.

How the risk is reduced

Screen materials for flammability across expected oxygen and airflow conditions. Provide extinguishing equipment.

🔔

Difficult detection

A faint flame can escape visual notice. Smoke must reach a sensor before it can trigger an alarm.

How the risk is reduced

Test detector response with representative particles and airflow. Provide audible and visible warnings.

🌡

Heat and equipment damage

Local heating can injure crew or damage wiring near the fire.

How the risk is reduced

Fire-resistant materials, electrical fault protection and access for suppression limit damage.

🧹

Persistent contamination

Smoke and gases can linger after visible burning stops.

How the risk is reduced

Filter particles, remove gaseous contaminants and monitor the atmosphere during recovery.

🚪

Limited escape

Crew depend on the spacecraft for breathable air and have few places to retreat.

How the risk is reduced

Emergency planning provides for module isolation, crew refuge and evacuation when required.

Safety research areas covered (count)

Why Saffire leads

Saffire covers five areas, including detection and cleanup at spacecraft scale. BASS covers three, with direct evidence on how solid flames go out. These counts describe the breadth of the cited work. They do not certify crew protection or establish suppression effectiveness.

Rank and programAreas countedEvidence behind the count
1　Saffire I–VIMaterial flammability, fire spread & heat, Combustion gases, Smoke & particles, Detection, Post-fire cleanupLarge-scale burns aboard uncrewed Cygnus linked flame growth and heat to gas and aerosol measurements. Researchers tested detection and post-fire cleanup equipment.
Saffire VI report, Tables 1 and 2 · Saffire IV–V findings
2　BASS / BASS-IIMaterial flammability, fire spread & heat, Extinction & suppression, Combustion gasesSolid-fuel experiments varied flow and oxygen, examined flame extinction and recorded combustion gases in the ISS glovebox.
BASS-II summary report, Table A.5 (printed p. 111)
=3　SAME / SAME-RSmoke & particles, DetectionSmoke from heated spacecraft materials was used to characterize particle sizes and evaluate detector response.
Spacecraft smoke detector study
=3　FLEX / FLEX-2Extinction & suppression, Combustion gasesFLEX droplet tests examined suppression and revealed cool burning after visible extinction. Cool-flame chemistry can produce CO and formaldehyde.
FLEX experiment · ISS research benefits
=3　SoFIE · GEL resultsMaterial flammability, fire spread & heat, Extinction & suppressionExperiments on heated acrylic spheres measured how flow and oxygen affected the boundary between sustained burning and extinction.
Published GEL flight results
=3　ACMEMaterial flammability, fire spread & heat, Smoke & particlesThe Burning Rate Emulator addressed material flammability. Other ACME investigations examined soot formation in gaseous flames.
